stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: An economist randomly selected 600 warehouse workers from all warehouse workers employed in a certain state. For each worker, the economist recorded whether the worker had completed a forklift safety certification and what the worker earned per hour. On average, the workers who had completed the certification earned higher hourly wages than the workers who had not.
choices: Completing the certification causes higher hourly wages for warehouse workers in the state.
Completing the certification causes higher hourly wages, but only for the 600 workers in the sample.
Completing the certification is associated with higher hourly wages for warehouse workers in the state.
Completing the certification is associated with higher hourly wages, but only for the 600 workers in the sample.
explanation: The economist only recorded what the workers had already done, and nobody was randomly assigned to complete the certification. That means you can claim an association but not a cause. The workers were randomly selected from all warehouse workers in the state, so you can apply the association to that whole population.

A.why: You took a clear wage gap as proof of cause. Nobody was randomly assigned to get certified, though. Workers who chose the course may differ in experience or motivation, so this observational study can't show cause.

B.why: You mixed up the two kinds of randomness. Narrowing the claim to the sample doesn't make a causal claim acceptable, because cause needs random assignment and this study had none.

D.why: You correctly stopped at association but missed that the 600 workers were randomly selected from every warehouse worker in the state. Random selection is what lets you generalize the result to the state.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A materials engineer took 80 steel bars from a single production batch. The engineer randomly assigned 40 of the bars to receive a new anti-corrosion coating and the other 40 to receive the standard coating. After 30 days in a salt-spray chamber, the bars with the new coating showed significantly less rust than the bars with the standard coating.
choices: The new coating causes less rusting than the standard coating for steel bars like those tested.
The new coating causes less rusting than the standard coating for steel bars from any manufacturer.
The new coating is associated with less rusting, but the study cannot show that the coating causes it.
No conclusion about cause is possible, because the bars were not randomly selected from all steel bars.
explanation: The bars were randomly assigned to the two coatings, so you can conclude that the new coating caused the difference in rust. The bars all came from one batch and were not randomly selected from a wider population, so the conclusion only covers bars like the ones tested.

B.why: You got the cause right but stretched it too far. All 80 bars came from one batch, so nothing in the study lets you generalize to steel from any manufacturer.

C.why: You missed the random assignment. When subjects are randomly assigned to treatments, you are allowed to make a cause-and-effect claim, so 'association only' is too weak.

D.why: You mixed up the two kinds of randomness. Random selection controls how far you can generalize, not whether you can claim a cause. Random assignment allows the causal claim, and this study had it.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: An agronomist randomly selected 120 plots from all wheat fields in a certain county. Of these plots, 60 were randomly assigned to receive a new nitrogen fertilizer, and the other 60 received no fertilizer. At harvest, the plots that received the fertilizer had a substantially higher mean yield than the plots that did not.
choices: The fertilizer is linked to higher yields in the county's wheat fields, but it cannot be shown to cause them.
The fertilizer causes higher yields in the 120 plots studied, but this cannot be extended to the county.
The fertilizer causes higher yields in wheat fields in this county and in wheat fields in every other county.
The fertilizer causes higher yields in wheat fields throughout the county from which the plots were chosen.
explanation: This study used both kinds of randomness. Random assignment to fertilizer or no fertilizer lets you claim a cause. Random selection from all the county's wheat fields lets you generalize to the county. Only this choice gets both parts right.

A.why: You missed that the plots were randomly assigned to receive the fertilizer. With random assignment, a cause-and-effect conclusion is allowed, not just an association.

B.why: You missed that the plots were randomly selected from all wheat fields in the county. That random selection lets you extend the result to the whole county.

C.why: You generalized past the population that was sampled. The plots came only from this county, so the study says nothing about other counties.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A hydrologist asked residents of a river valley to volunteer their private wells for testing, and 45 well owners agreed. For each well, the hydrologist measured the distance from the well to the river and the nitrate concentration in the well's water. Wells closer to the river tended to have lower nitrate concentrations.
choices: For the 45 wells tested, being closer to the river causes lower nitrate concentrations.
For the 45 wells tested, being closer to the river is associated with lower nitrate concentrations.
For all wells in the valley, being closer to the river is associated with lower nitrate concentrations.
For all wells in the valley, being closer to the river causes lower nitrate concentrations.
explanation: The hydrologist only measured wells as they already were, and nothing was randomly assigned, so you can only claim an association. The wells were volunteered rather than randomly selected, so the association applies only to the 45 wells tested.

A.why: You accepted a causal claim from an observational study. Nothing was randomly assigned, and other factors such as soil type or nearby farming could explain the pattern.

C.why: You generalized from a volunteer sample. Owners who chose to have their wells tested may not represent the valley, so the result can't be extended to all wells there.

D.why: You made both mistakes. You claimed cause without random assignment, and you generalized to the valley without random selection.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A city's transportation department identified 40 intersections where residents had complained about speeding. The department randomly assigned 20 of these intersections to have a raised crosswalk installed, and the other 20 were left unchanged. Six months later, the average driving speed had fallen by much more at the intersections with raised crosswalks.
choices: Raised crosswalks cause lower driving speeds at every intersection in the city, including those without complaints.
Raised crosswalks are associated with lower driving speeds, but the study cannot show that they cause them.
Raised crosswalks cause lower driving speeds at intersections similar to the 40 included in the study.
Falling driving speeds caused the department to install raised crosswalks at 20 of the 40 intersections.
explanation: The intersections were randomly assigned to get a raised crosswalk or not, so you can conclude that the crosswalks caused the drop in speed. The 40 intersections were chosen because of complaints, not randomly selected, so the conclusion only covers intersections like them.

A.why: You generalized beyond the intersections that were studied. Only intersections with speeding complaints were included, so the study can't speak for every intersection in the city.

B.why: You missed the random assignment. Because chance decided which intersections got crosswalks, a cause-and-effect claim is justified.

D.why: You reversed cause and effect. The crosswalks were assigned at random before speeds were measured, so falling speeds couldn't have decided where they went.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: An immunologist randomly selected 1,000 adults from a registry of all adult residents of a certain city. For each adult, the immunologist recorded the average number of hours the adult slept per night and measured the level of a certain antibody in the adult's blood. Adults who slept more hours per night tended to have higher antibody levels.
choices: Among adults in the city, sleeping more hours is associated with higher antibody levels.
Among adults in the city, sleeping more hours causes higher antibody levels.
Among adults in every city, sleeping more hours causes higher antibody levels.
Only among the 1,000 adults sampled is sleeping more associated with higher antibody levels.
explanation: The immunologist recorded how much people already slept and didn't assign sleep amounts, so you can claim only an association. The adults were randomly selected from all adults in the city, so the association applies to the city's adults.

B.why: You accepted a causal claim from an observational study. Nobody was assigned to sleep more, and factors such as age or general health could affect both sleep and antibody levels.

C.why: You made two errors. You claimed cause without random assignment, and you generalized to every city when the sample came from one city only.

D.why: You missed that the 1,000 adults were randomly selected from all adults in the city. Random selection lets you extend the association to that whole population.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A coach recruited 60 volunteer sprinters from college track teams. The coach randomly assigned 30 of the sprinters to an 8-week plyometric training program and the other 30 to their teams' usual training. On average, the sprinters in the plyometric program improved their 100-meter times by significantly more than the other sprinters did.
choices: The plyometric program causes greater improvement in sprint times for all athletes in every sport.
The plyometric program is associated with greater improvement, but it cannot be shown to cause it.
No cause-and-effect conclusion is possible, because the sprinters were volunteers, not a random sample.
The plyometric program causes greater improvement in sprint times for sprinters like those in the study.
explanation: The sprinters were randomly assigned to the two programs, so you can conclude that the plyometric program caused the extra improvement. They were volunteers rather than a random sample, so the conclusion only covers sprinters like the ones studied.

A.why: You generalized far past the sample. The study included only volunteer college sprinters, so it says nothing about athletes in other sports.

B.why: You missed the random assignment. When chance decides who gets the treatment, the study supports a causal conclusion, not just an association.

C.why: You mixed up the two kinds of randomness. Volunteers limit how far you can generalize, but random assignment still allows a causal claim about sprinters like these.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A meteorologist reviewed one year of records from 50 weather stations that had been chosen for a regional monitoring network. For each night, the meteorologist compared the amount of cloud cover with the overnight low temperature. At these stations, nights with more cloud cover tended to have higher overnight low temperatures.
choices: At these 50 stations, more cloud cover causes higher overnight low temperatures.
At these 50 stations, more cloud cover is associated with higher overnight low temperatures.
At these 50 stations, higher overnight low temperatures cause more cloud cover.
At weather stations worldwide, more cloud cover is associated with higher overnight lows.
explanation: The meteorologist only looked at existing records, and nothing was randomly assigned, so you can claim an association but not a cause. The stations were chosen for a regional network rather than randomly selected from stations worldwide, so the conclusion is limited to these 50 stations.

A.why: You accepted a causal claim because the pattern looked convincing. This is an observational study with no random assignment, so it can show only an association.

C.why: You reversed the direction and still made a causal claim. Observational records can't support a cause in either direction.

D.why: You generalized beyond the stations studied. They were picked for one regional network, not randomly selected from stations around the world.
